Para dibujar la imagen bastan dos de ell: Two of them are enough to draw the image: the ray parallel to the axis, which leaves passing through the focus (or as if coming from it); the ray that passes through the centre of the lens (or the vertex of the mirror), which is not deviated or is reflected at the same angle; and the ray aimed at the focus, which leaves parallel to the axis. The image is where they cross, or where their extensions would cross if it is virtual.

Con dos o más lentes se resuelve una det: With two or more lenses they are solved one after another: the image of the first is the object of the second. If the lenses are a distance $d$ apart and the first forms its image at $s′_1$, the object of the second is at $s_2 = d − s′_1$. If $s′_1 > d$ the image falls "behind" the second lens and behaves as a virtual object ($s_2 < 0$): the equation still holds without any change. Cuando la imagen intermedia cae justo en: When the intermediate image falls exactly at the focus of the next lens, the rays leave parallel (image at infinity) and that lens forms its own at its focal plane. For two thin lenses a distance $d$ apart, the combination is equivalent to a single lens of focal length $f$ with $1/f = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2 − d/(f_1 f_2)$; in contact ($d = 0$) the powers add. If $1/f = 0$ the system is afocal, like a telescope: a parallel beam leaves parallel. The compound microscope is the classic example: the objective forms a highly magnified real image that the eyepiece uses as a magnifying glass.
